PHSCS 587

MOS channel mobility

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows why carriers near an oxide interface encounter several competing scattering mechanisms

Effective channel mobility is a carrier-weighted average: μeff = ∫μ(x)n(x)dx / ∫n(x)dx across the inversion layer. It converts a nonuniform carrier distribution and local response into a useful transport parameter.

Phonons, charged impurities and interface roughness compete. A stronger normal field pulls inversion charge toward the interface, often increasing roughness scattering. For the empirical electron model, Eeff = (|Qd| + |Qi|/2)/εsi; the corresponding hole data use a one-third inversion-charge weighting. These weightings describe particular empirical mobility relationships.

The reading reports approximate high-temperature phonon-limited μeff ∝ T⁻³ᐟ². That is not a universal curve across all fields and temperatures. A Matthiessen model, 1/μeff ≈ Σᵢ1/μᵢ, is a useful independent-scattering approximation, rather than an exact rule for every channel.

Keep the two field directions visible in the device picture. The field normal to the gate controls confinement and the inversion layer’s exposure to the interface. The longitudinal source-to-drain field drives transport along the channel. Increasing gate bias and increasing drain bias therefore change different parts of the scattering and charge problem.

Example

If two illustrative independent mechanisms would each limit mobility to 600 cm²/(V·s), the inverse-mobility approximation gives μeff ≈ 300 cm²/(V·s), or 0.030 m²/(V·s).

Sources and scope
  • PHSCS 587 reading: 5.2, empirical universal mobility
  • PHSCS 587, 5.2 recording 1: effective normal field, strain, roughness and longitudinal-field effects.

Practice

1. Why can increasing VGS fail to produce the current increase predicted with constant mobility?

Track both inversion charge and proximity to the interface.

Higher gate voltage can increase inversion charge while also increasing the normal field and degrading effective mobility. The current response then reflects both changes.
